questions.q: When is real-time (synchronous) embedding generation the right choice?
options: When freshness is the product — e.g. a support agent that must search a ticket the moment it is filed — accepting synchronous latency and coupled failure modes
When the embedding provider offers no API
When documents never change
When cost is the dominant concern
questions.explain: Real-time is right when freshness is the product: new tickets or SKUs must be searchable immediately; the costs are synchronous latency, coupled failure modes, and per-request pricing with no batching discount.

questions.q: What hardening does the chapter require for the real-time write path?
options: Retry the embedding API forever inside the HTTP request
Drop the document if the embedding API times out
Cache the failure and return an error to the user

Never let an embedding failure lose the document: write the raw text first with a NULL embedding and an EmbeddingStatus = 'pending' flag, then fill it in — the document is never lost, only its searchability is delayed
questions.explain: The hardened pattern: persist the text first with NULL embedding and EmbeddingStatus = 'pending'; if the provider is down, the batch worker fills it in later — the document is never lost, only its searchability is delayed.

questions.q: How does the UPDATE TOP ... OUTPUT claim pattern let batch workers scale without an external queue?
options: It locks the whole table so only one worker runs at a time
Each worker atomically claims its batch, processes it, and writes results back — the status transition is the lock; crashed workers' 'processing' rows are reclaimed by a sweeper job after a timeout
It sends rows to a message broker automatically
It requires manual coordination through a distributed lock service
questions.explain: The claim pattern is SQL Server's answer to the queue-consumer problem: each worker atomically claims a batch via the status transition as the lock, workers run in parallel with no coordination, and a sweeper reclaims rows from crashed workers.

questions.q: What is the headline SLI for the embedding generation pipeline?
options: Queue depth
Embedding model version number
End-to-end lag: source change to searchable vector — trend it, not just the queue depth
Number of worker threads
questions.explain: The end-to-end lag from source change to searchable vector is the pipeline's headline SLI; queue depth, dead-letter growth, and oldest-pending age are the alerting signals behind it.

questions.q: In the hybrid architecture, how are urgent and bulk documents routed, and how do the paths avoid conflicts?
options: Bulk documents are never embedded
Urgent documents go synchronous, bulk imports/re-embeds go through the queue, and both paths write through the same MERGE upsert — last writer wins and the content hash prevents redundant API calls
All documents go through both paths and duplicates are deleted nightly
Urgent documents skip the database entirely
questions.explain: Production reality is hybrid: route by document priority (urgent synchronous, bulk through the queue), with one MERGE upsert underneath so ordering conflicts resolve to last writer wins and the content hash prevents redundant API calls.
